fields.connection: どんなに + V volitional form + が
examples: No matter how much I am criticized, I will not bend my convictions.
No matter how busy I am, I make time with my family a priority.
No matter how disadvantaged we are, we will keep taking on the challenge.
No matter how far away it is, I will definitely go to see you.
No matter how hard it rains, the match will be held as scheduled.
fields.explain:
Formal, rhetorical nuance; used to emphasize an unchanging position.
Usually not used for things that have already happened or to describe past facts; to describe actual facts, use ～ても/～たって.
が and とも are interchangeable; とも is more formal and suits written language and speeches.

• Meaning: “No matter how (much)…, (still)…”; emphasizes determination or an unchanging assertion in the face of a high degree of a condition.
• Has a strong nuance; often used in declarations, slogans, formal written language, or firm assertions.
• Usually followed by a main clause expressing volition, determination, or an unchanging evaluation.
fields.notes:
• With Aい it is rare in modern spoken language; choose A-くても if you want everyday naturalness.
• N + であろうが/とも is common with nouns such as 誰・相手・天候・逆境.
• Can be emphasized with たとえ: たとえどんなに～うが/とも、…
mistakes: Wrong conjugation of Aい: × 忙しいようが → correct: 忙しかろうが.
Wrong with Aな/N: × 不利だようが → correct: 不利であろうが/だろうが.
Used for something already completed → sounds forced: use ～ても instead. Example: × どんなに雨が強かろうが、昨日行った。

rows: どんなに<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われようが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Neutral, common; less of a “declaration” nuance
いかに<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>であろうが。
Highlights the supposition with たとえ
たとえ<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける。

fields.meaning: Only thanks to… can there be…
examples: Our company exists only thanks to our customers.
I truly feel that my happiness is possible only because of my family.
Business deals depend on trust.
This award is an achievement made possible by the team.
Without your health, there is no work. Don't overdo it.
His success came only through his hard work.
fields.explain:
Formal, positive; often appears in speeches, announcements, and words of thanks.
Often used with nouns such as: お客様,皆様,家族,仲間,支援,努力,信頼,健康,命.
Asserts a strong cause-and-effect relationship and emphasizes the foundation.

• Expresses the relationship “only with N1 can there be N2”; N1 is the prerequisite and foundation of N2.
• Nuance of gratitude and respect, acknowledging an indispensable role.
• Scope: attaches only to nouns; used often in speeches, words of thanks, and corporate slogans.
• Rhetorical structure: N1 is placed first to emphasize “thanks to…”.
fields.notes:
• This pattern is effective in slogans: 「安全あっての生産」「健康あっての挑戦」.
• Can be repeated in parallel: 「家族あっての私、仲間あってのチーム」。
• To make it less formal, it can be replaced with 「〜のおかげで」; to emphasize an essential condition, use 「〜なくして」.
mistakes: Using it directly with a verb: incorrect. It must be N + あっての + N.
Understanding it as “probably thanks to”: incorrect. 「あっての」 is a strong assertion of an essential condition.
Confusing it with 「おかげで」: 「あっての」 modifies a noun, has a formal nuance, and is a fixed structure.
Not keeping the correct order of N1 (foundation) → N2 (result): reversing them makes the meaning wrong.

rows: Modifies a noun; nuance of gratitude
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>あっての<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>
Used with V or N; emphasizes the condition necessary for the action to happen
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>があってこそ<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>く。
Usually expresses a concrete result; less formal
<ruby>皆<rt>みな</rt></ruby>さんのおかげで<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>した。
Implies a negative condition; strongly hypothetical
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なくして<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>なし。

fields.connection: V volitional form + が + V volitional form + が
examples: Whether it rains or the wind blows, the marathon will go ahead.
Whether it is high or low, we will not change this standard.
Whether you are a student or a working adult, the rules you must follow are the same.
Whether it is sunny or rainy, I go jogging every morning.
Whether you like it or not, you should see the work you are given through to the end.
Whether you pass or fail, it was worth taking on the challenge.
fields.explain:
Position: The phrase AうがBうが comes at the beginning of a sentence or in the middle, followed by a concluding clause (often expressing firmness or being unaffected).
Typical collocations after the pattern: 関係ない・問題ない・問わない・構わない・同じだ・変わらない・やり抜く・続ける・実施する など.
Formality: であろうが (formal/written language) > だろうが (spoken language). With Aい, use かろうが (a literary form).
Nuance: Strong; emphasizes determination or rules. Often used in announcements, speeches, policy documents, or statements expressing a position.
Parallel forms: Keep the word class and logic parallel: if A is N, B is also N; if A is V意向, B is also V意向.

• Main meaning: Presents two possibilities or opposites and asserts that the result or position does not change. “Whether A or B, (still)…”, “Regardless of A or B, …”.
• Pragmatic value: Emphasizes determination, disregard of conditions, or the consistency of a rule or judgment. Strong nuance, more formal than ordinary conversational patterns.
• Information structure: Clause Aうが Bうが (concessive–listing clause) + main clause (conclusion/view: 関係ない・問わない・変わらない・続ける・行う…).
• Restriction: A and B should be the same word class and correspond to or contrast with each other (高い↔低い, 晴れ↔雨, 行く↔やめる).
fields.notes:
• Rhythm: The repeated pattern “A…が B…が” creates a rhetorical rhythm, suitable for speeches, headlines, and slogans.
• Implicit negation: Often implies “not affected by condition A/B”. Therefore, the second clause rarely expresses an easily changing state.
• Combining with interrogative words: Can be extended to “誰であろうが・いつであろうが・どこであろうが…”, and can also be placed in parallel: “誰であろうが 何であろうが…”.
• Style: For a lighter or more conversational tone, consider 〜にしろ〜にしろ or 〜でも〜でも.
• Note the irregular i-adjective: いい → よい → よかろうが. Example: よかろうが 悪かろうが.
mistakes: Wrong form: using the dictionary form instead of the volitional/conjectural form. Incorrect: 高いが 安いが. Correct: 高かろうが 安かろうが.
Mixing word classes: A is V意向 and B is N + だろう (not parallel), which makes the sentence awkward. Keep the same word class or a clearly corresponding pair.
Confusing it with ～うが～まいが: the JLPT often sets traps with the pair “行こうが 行くまいが” (one verb, two possibilities) vs “晴れだろうが 雨だろうが” (two contrasting nouns). Distinguish their functions clearly.
いい → よかろう: Test takers often write “いいかろうが” (incorrect). Correct: よかろうが.
Nuance too strong: using it in casual conversation can sound stiff. In the exam, choose the pattern that fits the context: であれ/にしろ may be more natural.
Missing the concluding clause: the pattern usually needs a following clause to complete the concession–conclusion meaning. Avoid ending with “AうがBうが、…(left hanging)”.
Answer-choice traps: wrong answers often replace が with は/も/を or use “静かろうが” (wrong word class). Check the endings かろう/だろう/であろう and the 意向形.

fields.connection: V volitional form + と + V volitional form + と
examples: Whether it rains or the wind blows, the marathon will be held as planned.
Whether you cry or laugh, time will not wait for you.
Whether the price is high or low, quality comes first.
Whether you are a child or an adult, the rules are the same.
No matter how many objections there are, we will not change our policy.
Whether he comes or not, I will keep preparing.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes volition or determination: Often used to show a firm position that is not affected.
Formal/rhetorical: Suits speeches and written language; in everyday conversation it can be replaced with ～ても/～に関わらず.
Binary listing: The two possibilities should match in word class and degree (verb with verb, adjective with adjective...).
The second part rarely takes commands or requests: It is seldom used with direct requests; if it is, the tone is strong.

• Meaning: Emphasizes that “whether it is possibility A or possibility B, the result, determination, or judgment in the second clause does not change”.
• Character: Emphatic style, somewhat formal or oratorical; stronger than ～ても.
• Grammar: A and B are usually an opposing pair, two extremes, or two typical options. The following clause often goes with phrases such as 「関係ない」「影響されない」「同じだ」「構わない」「～してみせる」.
• Tense agreement: The second part is usually in the general present, expressing a general judgment or strong volition; it is rarely used for a small, momentary event.
fields.notes:
• Group 1 verbs into the volitional form: 書く→書こう, 行く→行こう, 読む→読もう; Group 2: 食べる→食べよう; 来る→来よう; する→しよう.
• i-adjectives: 高い→高かろう, 低い→低かろう. Nouns/na-adjectives: 学生だろう/学生であろう, 便利だろう/便利であろう (であろう is used in formal style).
• Often combined with emphatic words: たとえ～うと, いかに～うと, どれほど～うと.
• The second clause is usually a general judgment, a rule, a fact, or strong volition; avoid describing small, momentary events.
mistakes: Conjugation error: using “高いだろうと” instead of “高かろうと”; using “学生だと” instead of “学生だろうと/であろうと”.
Not parallel: combining different word classes or degrees: “雨が降ろうと高かろうと” (logically wrong).
Confusing it with ～うと～まいと: that pattern requires the contrast of doing/not doing the same verb; it cannot be replaced with a pair of other word classes.
Using it for trivial situations: avoid using it with momentary actions; choose ～ても instead.
JLPT: Often tests the conjugations “～かろうと/～であろうと” and comparison with “～に関わらず/～ても”.

examples: Despite the surgery, the patient could not be saved.
Even though I stayed up all night studying, I failed the exam.
Even though I searched everywhere, I couldn't find my wallet.
Even though we waited in line for a long time, the tickets were sold out.
Despite the parents' efforts, the plan was canceled.
fields.explain:
Placed in the cause clause indicating effort, followed by a negative or unwanted result.
Can be used in both formal and everyday contexts; “甲斐もなく/甲斐なく” is formal.
Has a strong emotional nuance; avoid it when you might hurt the listener in a sensitive situation.
Not combined with a command or suggestion in the second clause.
If you want to say “not worth doing”, 〜がいがない/〜甲斐がない is more natural when talking about potential value.

• Meaning: “Even though… was done, it was in vain / brought no result”, “despite the effort, the outcome was futile”.
• Nuance: Regret, disappointment, sadness; usually goes with a negative result.
• Pragmatics: Used to recount facts that did not turn out as hoped; avoid using it with commands or volition.
• Grammar: “かい” is a noun; it is preceded by Nの or Vた.
• Different from “むだに”: ～かいもなく is specifically tied to “effort/hard work”, not simply waste.
fields.notes:
• “甲斐” is a Sino-Japanese noun; adding “も” emphasizes total negation.
• Appears often in news and medical reports: 〜治療の甲斐もなく.
• Avoid overusing it in polite communication about sad news; you can switch to a more neutral expression.
• It can come at the beginning of a sentence or in the middle of one; it is usually followed by a comma and then the result clause. meaning_vi: Even though you tried, the result was regrettable ⏐ explain: Expresses the meaning that even if you try and make an effort, there is no result as hoped or expected…
1
手術 のかいもなく、愛犬が死んでしまった。 Despite the surgery, my beloved dog died.
2
予選で落ちてしまい、一生懸命 練習した かいがなかった。 I was eliminated in the preliminaries; all that hard practice was in vain.
mistakes: Used with a positive result: incorrect. ～かいもなく is used only when the result is bad or not as hoped.
Confusing it with ～てもむだ: one is a fact that has already happened; the other is a hypothetical judgment.
Dropping “の” after a noun: it must be Nのかいもなく, not Nかいもなく.
Spelling mistake: 甲斐 → miswritten as 貝/皆.
Combining it with a command or volition in the second clause: unnatural.

<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>したかいもなく、<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>。

examples: Besides working as a teacher, he also writes novels.
While studying management at university, I help out at my father's shop.
Alongside my research, I also take part in local volunteer activities.
While raising my children, I work as a translator from home.
Alongside my main job, I put out a podcast on weekends.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes main/secondary roles: A (before かたわら) is usually the main occupation, and B is an accompanying activity.
Duration: Suits activities that continue over a period; not used for two actions performed simultaneously in a brief moment.
Written language/introductions: Natural in résumés, articles, and career interviews; more polite and formal than ～ながら.

• Meaning: “Besides (the job/duty/activity) A, (in parallel) also does B.” Emphasizes that A is the main one and B is a secondary one over a period of time.
• Scope: Expresses an ongoing situation that is regular or periodic rather than a momentary action.
• Pragmatics: Often used in written language, profile introductions, biographies, and career descriptions: 仕事のかたわら, 研究するかたわら…
fields.notes:
• Part B can be a habit or regular activity: 「～もしている」「～も行っている」「～も続けている」.
• Not used with direct commands or volition: ×「勉強するかたわら、来なさい」.
• With the noun meaning “beside (physically)”: 「かたわらに」= “beside”: 「机のかたわらに鞄を置く」 (not the grammar point for parallel occupations).
• Often used with words for work or positions: 仕事／研究／育児／学業／本業 のかたわら.
mistakes: Using it for momentary actions: ×「歩くかたわら、電話に出た」→ use ～ながら instead.
No main/secondary relationship: if A and B are equal, consider using ～一方で or ～ながら.
Wrong word class: used only with N の / V-る; not used with an adjective directly before かたわら.
Confusing it with the positional meaning: 「かたわらに」 (beside) ≠ the grammar point “besides doing…, also…”.
JLPT: Often asks you to distinguish ～かたわら from ～ながら/～ついでに in terms of duration and the main/secondary relationship.

rows: Parallel over a long period; A is main, B is secondary.
<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby><ruby>員<rt>いん</rt></ruby>のかたわら、<ruby>作家<rt>さっか</rt></ruby><ruby>活動<rt>かつどう</rt></ruby>。
Two actions at the same time (immediate simultaneity) in one moment; neutral nuance, more colloquial.
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
Presents two contrasting or parallel aspects; does not emphasize “main/secondary”.
<ruby>都市<rt>とし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>な<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>物価<rt>ぶっか</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
Doing B while taking the opportunity of doing A; “secondary” by opportunity, not ongoing.
<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>のついでに<ruby>切手<rt>きって</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。

examples: This package weighs a good 20 kilos.
It's a good 5 kilometers from here to the station, you know.
That painting is worth tens of millions or more.
As many as a thousand spectators gathered at the venue.
A huge snake as long as 3 meters was found.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “larger than one thinks”; can carry a positive exaggerating nuance in advertising and headlines.
Usually not used with small numbers, because the emphasis is lost.
Can be used both as a predicate and as a noun modifier: 〜からある／〜からのN.

• Emphasizes a large degree, beyond the usual: “as much as, about, at least”.
• Used with a specific number + unit; often carries a nuance of surprise or emphasis.
• Choose the right suffix: からある (size/weight/length), からする (price), からの (modifying a large quantity).
• Often used in descriptions, advertising, and the press to emphasize scale.
fields.notes:
• When modifying a noun, use 「〜からのN」 so that the sentence flows more naturally.
• In the media, this phrase often comes with estimated numbers: 数百、数千、数十万… to heighten the effect.
• For area/volume, 「からある」 can also be used if the focus is on “large scale”.
mistakes: Used with a small number (1キロからある): sounds forced. Use it when the number feels “large”.
Confusing the scope: for prices you must use 「からする」, not 「からある」.
Forgetting to add a noun when using 「からの」: you need 「数百人からの応募」; it does not stand alone.
Misunderstanding it as “at least”: although the meaning is close, the focus is on emphasizing size/significance, not a purely mathematical lower bound.

<ruby>百人<rt>ひゃくにん</rt></ruby>からの<ruby>応募<rt>おうぼ</rt></ruby>

examples: The renovation will cost several million yen or more.
I hear that painting costs several million yen or more.
They say the latest model costs a thousand dollars or more.
I take good care of my lens, which cost several hundred thousand yen.
The membership fee and facility fee apparently come to tens of thousands of yen or more.
He wears suits that cost hundreds of thousands of yen.
fields.explain:
Common in advertising, news, and product or project evaluations; conveys an impression of how expensive something is.
Placed before a noun for emphasis: 〜からするN; placed at the end of a sentence to conclude about the price.
Used with vague numbers:数十／数百／何＋単位to make it more evocative.

• Used to indicate “a price/cost of at least about …”, creating a sense of large/expensive.
• When used as a modifier, からする attaches after the counter to emphasize how “huge” the following N is.
• Typical scope: money, costs, financial value; rarely used for physical size.
fields.notes:
• In PR writing, からする heightens the sense of “luxury/expensiveness”.
• Used with nouns for cost items: 予算／費用／投資／被害額.
• In headlines: 「〜からする被害」 emphasizes the scale of the damage.
mistakes: Used for size instead of money: ×5キロからする道 → ○5キロからある道.
Confusing it with からの when modifying a number of people: ×100人からする観客 → ○100人からの観客.
Using it with a small amount of money makes the sentence sound odd or conveys the wrong emotion.
JLPT: recognize “a large price / at least” → choose からする rather than 以上/からの/からある.
